questions.question: Q1. In Sub-Calc A the linear law θ_lin = κL is corrected by θ = θ_lin/(1 + β·θ_lin²) with β = 0.0534 rad⁻². What is the physical meaning of this rolloff?

answers.b: It models geometric stiffening that makes equal pressure steps add ever less angle past ~30°.
answers.c: It accounts for air leakage from the cavity.
answers.d: It adds thermal expansion to the finger.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Unit conversion is separate; β carries physical stiffening.
explanations.b: Correct — The moment arm no longer stays constant at large curl, so the angle saturates below the linear prediction.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Leakage is not part of this bending model.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Temperature is not in Sub-Calc A.

questions.question: Q2. The finger uses E = 1 MPa and I_eff = 1.82×10⁻¹⁰ m⁴. If you doubled the cavity eccentricity d_ecc at fixed pressure and area, how would the curvature κ change?

answers.a: It would roughly double, since M ∝ d_ecc and κ = M/(E·I_eff).

explanations.a: Correct — M scales linearly with d_ecc, and κ is proportional to M, so κ roughly doubles (before rolloff).
explanations.b: Incorrect — Larger eccentricity increases, not decreases, the moment.
explanations.c: Incorrect — κ depends directly on the moment arm.
explanations.d: Incorrect — A larger arm gives more curvature, not none.

questions.question: Q3. In Sub-Calc B, the finger is bent warm to θ_bent, then cooled. What must happen before the pressure is released for the shape to lock?

answers.a: The pressure must first be doubled.
answers.b: The finger must be heated further above T_g.
answers.c: The temperature must fall below T_g = 40 °C so the polymer vitrifies.
answers.d: The shape fixity R_f must be set to 0.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Extra pressure does not lock the shape.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Heating keeps it soft and it would spring back.
explanations.c: Correct — Only after crossing T_g does E jump to the glassy value and hold θ_held = R_f·θ_bent.
explanations.d: Incorrect — R_f = 0 would retain none of the bend.

questions.question: Q4. A pneumatic hold leaks power at P·Q_leak while an SMP lock holds at 0 W. For a finger held at P_bend = 60 kPa with Q_leak = 1×10⁻⁶ m³/s, what is the engineering trade-off the lock exploits?

answers.a: The lock is faster to actuate.
answers.b: The lock trades a one-time cooling step for continuous holding power that the pneumatic hold must keep spending.
answers.c: The lock needs no material at all.
answers.d: The lock increases the bending angle.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Speed is not the advantage; standing power is.
explanations.b: Correct — Vitrifying once removes the perpetual P·Q_leak leak of a pneumatic hold — the genuine 4D advantage.
explanations.c: Incorrect — It relies specifically on the SMP skin.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Locking preserves, it does not amplify, the bend.

questions.question: Q5. The crawl model gives δ_net = δ_ext·(1 − 1/μ_asym). If μ_fwd = 0.6 and μ_back = 0.3, what happens?

answers.b: μ_asym = 2, so it crawls forward twice as fast.
answers.c: δ_net = δ_ext, full forward stroke retained.
answers.d: μ_asym = 0.5, so δ_net is negative and the robot crawls backward.

explanations.b: Incorrect — The ratio is 0.5, not 2, because back friction is the smaller one here.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Full retention would need μ_asym → ∞.
explanations.d: Correct — μ_asym = 0.3/0.6 = 0.5 gives (1 − 1/0.5) = −1, a negative net displacement.

questions.question: Q6. Why does a smooth 4D-printed surface represent a failure case for the crawling robot?

answers.a: Because μ_fwd ≈ μ_back gives μ_asym ≈ 1 and δ_net ≈ 0 — the robot oscillates without translating.
answers.b: Because it is too rough to slide on.
answers.c: Because the surface melts the polymer.
answers.d: Because friction becomes zero in both directions.

explanations.a: Correct — Equal directional friction cancels the net stroke; printed scales or angled legs are needed to break symmetry.
explanations.b: Incorrect — The problem is that it is too symmetric, not too rough.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Friction is present but symmetric, which is the actual issue.

questions.question: Q7. For the three-finger gripper, the max holdable mass is m_max = 3·F_grasp·μ/g. At fixed pressure, increasing θ toward 90° does what to m_max?

answers.c: Decreases it toward zero, because F_grasp = P·A_tip·cosθ collapses.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Reach (R_max) grows with sinθ, but holding force falls with cosθ.
explanations.b: Incorrect — m_max tracks F_grasp, which changes with θ.
explanations.c: Correct — cosθ → 0 drives F_grasp and therefore m_max to zero near 90°.
explanations.d: Incorrect — At 90° the force and holdable mass vanish.

questions.question: Q8. The gripper workspace runs R_min = r_palm to R_max = r_palm + L·sinθ. What is the design tension between grip strength and reach as θ increases?

answers.a: There is none; both improve together.
answers.b: Reach and grip both fall with θ.
answers.c: Larger θ shrinks reach and strengthens grip.
answers.d: Larger θ extends reach (sinθ up) but weakens the grip (cosθ down), so reach and holding force trade off.

explanations.a: Incorrect — The sinθ and cosθ dependencies pull in opposite directions.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Reach rises with θ even as grip falls.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Reach grows, not shrinks, with sinθ.
explanations.d: Correct — sinθ grows the workspace while cosθ cuts the grasp force — a direct trade-off.

questions.question: Q9. In Sub-Calc E the plant is G(s) = K_plant/(τ_p·s + 1) with K_plant = 1.4 °/kPa. If K_p is pushed very high, what failure mode appears in the step response?

answers.b: The loop rings with large overshoot and may saturate the 150 kPa valve limit or fail to settle.
answers.c: The response becomes perfectly critically damped.

explanations.a: Incorrect — High K_p reduces steady error; it worsens overshoot instead.
explanations.b: Correct — Too much proportional gain produces ringing and can hit the valve rail without settling.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Excess gain under-damps rather than critically damps the loop.
explanations.d: Incorrect — K_plant is a fixed plant property, not gain-dependent.

questions.question: Q10. The PID controller meets spec at overshoot < 15 % and settling < 2 s, yet the model note warns the gains are only a starting point. Why?

answers.a: Because the first-order linear plant ignores the real finger's nonlinear, hysteretic saturation seen in Sub-Calc A.
answers.b: Because PID control never works on real hardware.
answers.c: Because the valve limit is set too high.
answers.d: Because the setpoint is always wrong.

explanations.a: Correct — The linear model over-predicts on large steps where the actual finger stiffens and lags, so on-hardware retuning is expected.
explanations.b: Incorrect — PID does work; the caution is about model fidelity, not the method.
explanations.c: Incorrect — The 150 kPa clamp is physical, not the source of the caveat.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The setpoint is user-chosen and not inherently wrong.
